newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM DENIES UNHAPPY EBRD TOP JOB MAY GO TO U.S.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM DENIES UNHAPPY EBRD TOP JOB MAY GO TO U.S.

text.p: Belgium denied on Tuesday a report its staff at the London-based European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) were in revolt over the appointment of a new vice-president.

The London Times reported on Tuesday that Belgian staff were insisting a senior Belgian official gets the job of Ron Freeman, a former Wall Street banker who is leaving after six years as the EBRD's number two.
"There is no Belgian plot or revolt," Bernard Snoy, Belgium's representative on the EBRD's 23-member supervisory board of directors told Reuters.
"Our position is that we regret the departure of Mr Freeman...and we fully support the process set up by (President Jacques de Larosiere) to secure good candidates," Snoy added.
Snoy said that contrary to the report the board had not been asked to chose a replacement for Freeman at a meeting on Tuesday as a number of U.S. candidates had withdrawn their applications.

"Mr Freeman has agreed to stay on a few more weeks," Snoy said, while the search goes on. "If after a long period of time the U.S. cannot come up with a candidate then its probable that Mr de Larosiere would have to submit another name but its too early to speculate on that."
A senior official in Brussels denied also there was any unhappiness at the way the EBRD was being run.
Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt was likely to express full support for de Larosiere at the bank's annual general meeting of the 55-shareholders in London on April 14.
De Larosiere's four-year appointment is due to end in the autumn. "We hope he decides to stay on," one Belgian official said. "That shows the degree of confidence we have in him."
The EBRD was set up 1991 to help east European nations build up their economies after the collapse of the Soviet bloc.

De Larosiere, a former International Monetary Fund president, was appointed after the bank's first president, Frenchman Jacques Attali, was forced to resign over lavish expenditure on its London headquarters.

The bank's shareholders approved last year doubling its capital to 20 billion European Currency Units (Ecus), because loans have now reached 9.96 billion Ecus. But this has not yet happened because of delays in ratifying the decision.
Belgium and Luxembourg are among the countries that have not yet ratified the decision. Officials said, however, that the procedure in both countries was well in hand.
